cues.text: Let's turn now to a practical exercise: the AeroFreight metrics and defect tracking lab.

Here we take the ideas of measurement and apply them to a concrete scenario, so you can see how the numbers are actually worked out and, just as importantly, how they should and should not be interpreted.
We begin with definitions.
First, business lead time.
Business lead time is the date the change was deployed, minus the date it was requested.
Second, cycle time.
Under the convention we are using in this lab, cycle time is the date deployed, minus the date development started.
Notice the phrase "under lab convention." Different organizations draw these lines in different places, so we are telling you plainly which definition this lab uses.
That brings us to a caution about DORA.
DORA's change lead time is generally measured from commit to production.
That is not identical to business lead time, which starts from the moment of the request.
So whenever you report one of these metrics, you must explicitly state the metric definition you are using.
Otherwise two people can say "lead time" and mean quite different things.
Third, defect density.
Defect density equals defects divided by thousands of lines of code, written as KLOC.
K-L-O-C simply means one thousand lines of code.
Now the lab scenario.
The change was requested on March 1.
Development started on March 20.
It was deployed on March 25.
The system has fifteen thousand lines of code, and there were forty-five critical production defects.
Let's work through it.
Lead time is March 1 to March 25, which is twenty-four elapsed days.
Cycle time is March 20 to March 25, which is five days.
The difference between them is the pre-development wait: from March 1 to March 20, nineteen days.
Check that the pieces fit: nineteen plus five gives twenty-four.
For defect density, we first convert fifteen thousand lines of code into KLOC, which is fifteen.
Then forty-five defects divided by fifteen KLOC gives three defects per KLOC.
Now, what do we conclude?
The long wait, nineteen of twenty-four days before development even began, suggests that we should investigate approvals, queues, and dependencies.
But be careful: this is not proof of bureaucracy alone.
The number tells us where to look, not what the cause is.
Likewise, defect density depends on the programming language, the counting rules, the scope and severity of defects included, and how the software is used.
So do not compare defect density figures blindly across projects or teams.
Here is the same calculation expressed in Python.
The code is shown for explanation; we are not claiming it was executed here.
The first line, from datetime import date, brings in the date type from Python's standard datetime module.
Then three variables are created. requested is date of 2026, 3, 1. started is date of 2026, 3, 20. deployed is date of 2026, 3, 25.

Next, lead is set to deployed minus requested, then dot days, which subtracts two dates to get a duration and reads its number of days. cycle is deployed minus started, dot days. density is 45 divided by, in parentheses,
15000 divided by 1000, which is the lines of code converted to KLOC.
Finally, an assert statement checks that the tuple lead, cycle, density equals twenty-four, five, and three point zero.
If any value differed, the assertion would raise an error.
Here it is simply stating the expected results: lead twenty-four, cycle five, density three point zero.
Finally, how should we use these metrics?
They should guide improvement, not just decorate a report.
Identify the stages where work waits.
Assign an owner to each problem.
Reduce unnecessary approvals, while preserving the controls that are genuinely required.
Improve the quality gates, and monitor trends over time rather than a single snapshot.
Record your evidence, and avoid inventing performance results you have not measured.
For critical defects specifically, trace each one back to its requirement and to the tests that should have caught it.
Verify fixes before closing the defect, and hold a postmortem to learn from what happened.
And remember the larger point: documentation and collaboration connect the entire SDLC, from the first request to the final deployment and beyond.
